At emergence, a newly hatched chick weighs just 3.05 grams [Ww0 = 3.05 grams], representing a remarkably small initial wet weight that implies considerable reliance on yolk reserves during the first few days of life. This altricial nestling, brooded constantly by both parents, grows rapidly within the humid cave environment that buffers extreme external temperatures.

Under the species' typical active metabolic body temperature of 38.1 Â°C [T = 38.1 Â°C], the nestling attains flight capability after 54 days since birth [tx = 54 days since birth]. This fledging period is relatively protracted for a swift of this mass, likely reflecting the energetic constraints of foraging on patchy aerial prey in tropical rainforest. The fledgling then enters a post-natal phase of independence, developing flight muscles and honing its echolocation abilities used to navigate the dark caverns. This period between leaving the nest and achieving sexual maturity is a critical window of high juvenile mortality, a pattern common among aerially insectivorous birds.

Sexual maturity, or the onset of puberty as indicated by completed gonadal development, is reached at 162 days since birth [tp = 162 days since birth] under a body temperature of 38.1 Â°C [T = 38.1 Â°C]. This relatively rapid maturation for a bird of its size permits swiftlets to enter the breeding population early in their second calendar year. Following puberty, the first successful brood is initiated at 365 days since birth [tR = 365 days since birth], also at a metabolic temperature of 38.1 Â°C [T = 38.1 Â°C], a timing closely matching that recorded for the common swift Apus apus. The delay between puberty and first reproduction may reflect the time required to establish a breeding territory within a dense colony and to construct the valuable, entirely salivary nest.

Reproductive output is low but consistent with a slow life-history strategy; females produce a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch] and typically raise one to two clutches per year [F_R_i = one to two clutches per year]. This yields an annual reproductive output of up to two eggs per year, a value that underscores the high energetic cost of producing the edible nest. Adult females reach an ultimate wet weight of 16.8 grams [Wwi = 16.8 grams], and the species' maximum recorded longevity in the wild is 16 years [am = 16 years] at 38.1 Â°C [T = 38.1 Â°C], a lifespan that considerably exceeds predictions based on body size alone and fits a pattern of delayed senescence in colonial, low-fecundity species.

The combination of a long lifespan, modest clutch size, and delayed first reproduction suggests an overall slow pace of life, with demographic resilience dependent on high adult survivorship. At the typical body temperature of 38.1 Â°C [T = 38.1 Â°C], the annual reproductive output is essentially one to two eggs per year, reflecting the single-egg clutch and extended interval between nesting attempts. This low annual output renders the species vulnerable to overharvesting of nests for bird's nest soup, as population recovery following disturbance is inherently slow. Conservation strategies therefore must prioritise the protection of breeding colonies from human exploitation and habitat degradation to sustain viable populations of this ecologically specialised cave-dweller.
